subject: Chem
title: Electrolysis, energy & reactions
sub: Electrolysis, exothermic and endothermic reactions, rates of reaction, reversible reactions and redox
strategyIntro: Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences tests chemistry alongside biology and physics: a multiple-choice paper (40 questions, 45 min), a theory paper of structured questions, and a practical or alternative-to-practical paper. Your school test may be shorter, but it will be marked the same way.

strategy.title: Multiple choice
points: About a minute per question. If one is taking longer, mark it and move on.
Cross out options you know are wrong first. Two often look similar: read every word.
Never leave one blank. A wrong answer loses nothing.

strategy.title: Structured questions
points: Marks go to keywords. Write the textbook term: “effervescence” or “fizzing”, not “it reacts”.
The marks in brackets tell you how many separate points to make.
Equations: check every atom balances, and add state symbols when the question asks.

strategy.title: Questions on experiments
points: Results tables: units go in the column headings, not next to each number.
Colour changes need both colours: “blue to white”, not just “white”.
Know the control variables and one safety precaution for each experiment.

strategy.title: Easy marks people lose
points: Saying ionic bonds “share” electrons. Ionic = transfer; covalent = share.
Writing “chlorine” when you mean the chloride ion, or “clear” when you mean “colourless”.
Calculations without units, or without the working shown.

commandWords: Give a short fact. No explanation needed.
Say what happens or what you see. With data, quote figures and units.
Say why or how. Use “because” and link cause to effect.
Apply what you know to a new situation. Any sensible reason scores.
Give similarities or differences for both things in the same sentence.
Show working and give the unit.
quizIntro: Answer in Paper 1 style: about a minute each, eliminating wrong options first. Read the explanation after every answer, even when you get it right.
flashIntro: These are close to Cambridge’s own wording. Say each definition out loud before you tap, then check you used the exact keywords. Cards marked (Extended) are Supplement content.

flashcards.back: The decomposition of an ionic compound, when molten or in aqueous solution, by the passage of an electric current.
A molten or aqueous ionic substance that conducts electricity and is decomposed by it.
Anode = positive electrode. Cathode = negative electrode.
Positive ions (cations, e.g. metal ions and H⁺) move to the cathode. Negative ions (anions) move to the anode.
Electrodes that do not react during electrolysis, usually graphite (carbon) or platinum.
A compound of two elements, e.g. lead(II) bromide. The metal forms at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode.
Lead (silvery liquid metal) at the cathode; bromine (red-brown vapour) at the anode.
Hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode; sodium hydroxide is left in solution. Hydrogen forms, not sodium, because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen.
Hydrogen at the cathode, oxygen at the anode, in a 2 : 1 volume ratio.
Cathode: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb (reduction). Anode: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ (oxidation).
A reaction that transfers thermal energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases. ΔH is negative.
A reaction that takes in thermal energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases. ΔH is positive.
Combustion of fuels, neutralisation, reaction of metals with acids, respiration.
Thermal decomposition (e.g. of calcium carbonate), photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium nitrate in water.
The transfer of thermal energy during a reaction, measured in kJ/mol.
Products are at a lower energy level than the reactants. The arrow for ΔH points down.
Products are at a higher energy level than the reactants. The arrow for ΔH points up.
The minimum energy that colliding particles must have to react. Shown as the hump from the reactants up to the peak.
Breaking bonds takes in energy (endothermic). Making bonds releases energy (exothermic).
ΔH = energy taken in to break bonds − energy released making bonds. Negative answer = exothermic.
How fast reactants are used up or products are made: the change in amount per unit time.
Higher concentration of a reactant in solution → faster reaction.
Higher temperature → faster reaction.
Smaller pieces (powder) have a larger surface area → faster reaction.
For reactions of gases, higher pressure → faster reaction (particles are closer together).
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction and is chemically unchanged at the end.
Steeper gradient = faster rate. The curve levels off when one reactant has been used up. Same amounts of reactants give the same final amount of product.
Measure volume of gas with a gas syringe, loss of mass on a balance, or time for a cross under the flask to disappear (precipitate forms). Take readings at regular time intervals.
Particles react only when they collide with at least the activation energy. Rate depends on the frequency of successful collisions.
Particles have more kinetic energy: they collide more often, and a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or above the activation energy.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful.
A chemical change makes a new substance and is often hard to reverse. A physical change (melting, dissolving) makes no new substance.
A reaction in which the products can react to form the original reactants again. Symbol: ⇌
Heating blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate gives white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate and water. Adding water turns it blue again and gives out heat.
Pink when hydrated, blue when anhydrous. Heating turns it blue; adding water turns it pink again.
In a closed system, the forward and reverse reactions happen at the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.
Gain of oxygen by a substance.
Loss of oxygen by a substance.
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen at the same time. E.g. CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O: copper(II) oxide is reduced, hydrogen is oxidised.
Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain of electrons. “OIL RIG”.
An oxidising agent oxidises another substance and is itself reduced. A reducing agent reduces another substance and is itself oxidised.

quiz.q: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed. What forms at the cathode?
quiz.why: Positive lead ions are attracted to the negative cathode and gain electrons to form lead. Bromine forms at the anode.

quiz.q: Why must an ionic compound be molten or dissolved before it can be electrolysed?
options: So the ions are free to move to the electrodes
So the electrodes do not corrode
So electrons can flow through the liquid
So it reaches a high enough temperature
quiz.why: In a solid the ions are fixed in the lattice. Melting or dissolving lets them move. The current is carried by ions in the electrolyte, not electrons.

quiz.q: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the anode?
quiz.why: Chloride ions go to the positive anode and form chlorine gas. Hydrogen forms at the cathode; sodium is never produced from the solution.

quiz.q: Which statement about the cathode is correct?
quiz.why: The cathode is negative, so positive ions move to it. Chlorine and other non-metals form at the positive anode.

quiz.q: (Extended) Which half-equation shows what happens at the cathode when molten sodium chloride is electrolysed?
quiz.why: At the cathode positive ions gain electrons (reduction): Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na. The chloride equation happens at the anode.

quiz.q: During a reaction the temperature of the solution falls from 21 °C to 15 °C. What type of reaction is it?
quiz.why: The reaction took thermal energy from the solution, so it got colder: endothermic. Neutralisation and combustion are exothermic.

quiz.q: Which of these is endothermic?
options: Neutralising an acid with an alkali
quiz.why: Thermal decomposition needs continuous heating to break the compound down, so it takes energy in. The others release energy.

quiz.q: On a reaction pathway diagram for an exothermic reaction, where are the products?
options: At a lower energy level than the reactants
At the same energy level as the reactants
At a higher energy level than the reactants
At the top of the activation energy hump
quiz.why: Energy has been given out to the surroundings, so the products have less energy than the reactants.

quiz.q: (Extended) Which statement about breaking chemical bonds is correct?
options: It happens only when a catalyst is present
quiz.why: Breaking bonds always needs energy (endothermic). Energy is released when new bonds form.

quiz.q: (Extended) H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies (kJ/mol): H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431. What is ΔH?
quiz.why: Breaking: 436 + 242 = 678. Making: 2 × 431 = 862. ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol. Remember there are two H–Cl bonds.

quiz.q: Marble chips react with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which change would NOT increase the rate?
options: Using a larger volume of the same acid
quiz.why: Extra acid of the same concentration does not make particles collide more often. Powder, heat and concentration all increase the rate.

quiz.q: A graph of volume of gas against time levels off. Why?
options: The catalyst has been used up
One of the reactants has been used up
quiz.why: When a reactant runs out, no more gas is made. Catalysts are not used up.

quiz.q: Which is the best description of a catalyst?
options: A substance that speeds up a reaction and is chemically unchanged at the end
A reactant that is added in excess
A substance that slows a reaction down
A substance that increases the amount of product made
quiz.why: A catalyst only changes how fast the product forms, not how much. It is not used up.

quiz.q: Why does magnesium powder react faster with acid than a magnesium ribbon of the same mass?
options: Powder has a larger surface area, so collisions are more frequent
quiz.why: More atoms are exposed to the acid, so there are more collisions per second.

quiz.q: (Extended) Why does increasing the temperature increase the rate of a reaction?
options: There are more particles in the same volume
Particles move faster, collide more often, and more collisions have energy ≥ activation energy
quiz.why: Temperature changes particle energy, not the activation energy. Lowering activation energy is what a catalyst does.

quiz.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
quiz.why: Rusting makes a new substance (hydrated iron(III) oxide). The others change state or dissolve: no new substance.

quiz.q: Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated. What colour change is seen?
quiz.why: Heating removes the water of crystallisation, leaving white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. Pink/blue is cobalt(II) chloride.

quiz.q: In 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, what happens to the magnesium?
options: It is reduced because it gains oxygen
It is neither oxidised nor reduced
It is oxidised because it gains oxygen
quiz.why: Gain of oxygen is oxidation. Reduction is loss of oxygen.

quiz.q: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Which substance is reduced?
quiz.why: Iron(III) oxide loses its oxygen, so it is reduced. Carbon monoxide gains oxygen, so it is oxidised.

quiz.q: (Extended) Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. Which statement is correct?
options: Chlorine is reduced and is the oxidising agent
Bromide ions are the oxidising agent
quiz.why: Each chlorine atom gains an electron (reduction), so chlorine is the oxidising agent. Bromide ions lose electrons and are oxidised.

examIntro: Theory-paper style. Write your answer first, then open the mark scheme and give yourself one mark per point you made clearly. One point per mark is the rule.

exam.q: Molten potassium iodide is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Name the product at each electrode.
points: Cathode: potassium
Anode: iodine

exam.q: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Name the gas formed at each electrode and give a test for each gas.
points: Cathode: hydrogen
Test: lighted splint gives a squeaky pop
Anode: oxygen
Test: relights a glowing splint

exam.q: Describe what happens when concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Explain why sodium is not produced.
points: Hydrogen gas forms at the cathode
Because hydrogen is less reactive than sodium (H⁺ ions are discharged, not Na⁺)
Chlorine gas forms at the anode, from chloride ions
Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper
Sodium hydroxide is left in the solution
(Extended) 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ and 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻

exam.q: State what is meant by an exothermic reaction and by an endothermic reaction.
points: Exothermic: transfers thermal energy to the surroundings (temperature rises)
Endothermic: takes in thermal energy from the surroundings (temperature falls)

exam.q: A student adds magnesium ribbon to dilute hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises from 20.0 °C to 31.5 °C. (a) Calculate the temperature change. (b) State the type of reaction and give a reason. (c) Suggest why a polystyrene cup is used.
points: (b) Exothermic
(b) Because the temperature increased / thermal energy was given out
(c) Polystyrene is an insulator, so less thermal energy is lost to the surroundings

exam.q: (Extended) Methane burns in oxygen in an exothermic reaction. Describe the reaction pathway diagram for this reaction, including the axes and all the labels needed.
points: y-axis energy, x-axis progress of reaction
Reactants (CH₄ + 2O₂) on the left at a higher level
Products (CO₂ + 2H₂O) on the right at a lower level
Curve rises to a peak then falls to the products
Activation energy: arrow from reactants up to the peak
ΔH: arrow from reactants down to products, labelled negative

exam.q: State two ways of increasing the rate of reaction between zinc and dilute sulfuric acid.
points: Increase the temperature
Use more concentrated acid
Use zinc powder / smaller pieces
Add a catalyst (e.g. copper(II) sulfate)

exam.q: Describe an experiment to find how the rate of reaction between marble chips (calcium carbonate) and dilute hydrochloric acid changes with time.
points: Collect the carbon dioxide in a gas syringe (or measure loss of mass on a balance)
Start the stopwatch as the reactants are mixed
Record volume (or mass) at regular time intervals, e.g. every 30 s
Plot a graph of volume (or mass) against time
Steeper gradient = faster rate; rate is fastest at the start

exam.q: (Extended) Use collision theory to explain why (a) increasing the concentration of acid and (b) adding a catalyst both increase the rate of a reaction.
points: (a) More reacting particles in the same volume
(a) So collisions are more frequent
(a) More successful collisions per second
(b) Catalyst provides an alternative pathway
(b) With a lower activation energy
(b) So a greater proportion of collisions have enough energy to react
exam.note: Any 5. Say “more frequent” or “per second”, not just “more collisions”.

exam.q: State what is meant by a reversible reaction and give the symbol used in equations.
points: The products can react to form the original reactants again / the reaction can go in both directions

exam.q: Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals are heated in a test tube. The solid left is cooled and then water is added to it. Describe what is seen at each stage.
points: On heating, blue crystals turn white
Droplets of water / steam given off (condense near the top of the tube)
When water is added, the white solid turns blue again
The tube gets hot when water is added (exothermic)

exam.q: When hydrogen is passed over heated copper(II) oxide: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O. Explain why this is a redox reaction and describe what is seen.
points: Copper(II) oxide loses oxygen
So copper(II) oxide is reduced
Hydrogen gains oxygen
So hydrogen is oxidised
Both happen at the same time, so it is redox
Black solid turns pink-brown (copper)
Droplets of water / condensation form
